newsitem.title: EGYPT: Flemings wants share in Egyptian GDR business.
newsitem.headline: Flemings wants share in Egyptian GDR business.

text.p: The London-based investment bank Flemings wants a share of the market for arranging GDRs in Egyptian stocks and is setting up a research team specialising in the Egyptian market, a director of the bank said.

Sir Peter de la Billiere, British Gulf War commander turned banker, told Reuters in an interview on Sunday evening that the bank would also probably set up a permanent presence in Cairo but he could not say when this would be.

Flemings missed out on the first three issues of global depositary receipts (GDRs) in Egyptian stocks, which were arranged by ING Barings, Salomon Brothers and then HSBC James Capel in conjunction with Nomura Securities.

"We are interested in any new GDRs that are coming along and we will certainly be doing all we can to play our part and hope that our commitment to Egypt will be rewarded with some of the business," said de la Billiere.

"There's a lot of business and no one bank, however big, can expect to have it to itself. We are going hard for a fair share of that business," added the banker, who had talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Sunday. At this stage Flemings has no specific GDRs in the pipeline, he said.

"We find Egypt an extremely interesting and attractive place to do business in and full of opportunities... So we are creating a substantial research team covering the major areas of Egyptian industry," he said.
"We are enthusiastically committed...and if that requires a permanent presence on the ground (in Egypt), which it probably will, then we will provide that," he added.
But de la Billiere said the Egyptian authorities had to show that the stock market met international legal standards.

"It's got to be seen to be working before outside investors are going to have full confidence. It needs tidying up and people to see that it is really effective as well as being there in skeleton form," he said. He did not elaborate.

But Ossama Nasser, head of Middle East operations for Flemings, said he was fully satisfied with the legal framework and remained bullish about the prospects for the Egyptian market despite the recent end of a long bull run.
"There is no problem. The legal framework is very suitable and the environment is so encouraging that really one can not look at it negatively at all," he said.

"You are going to get these corrections in any market. I think Egypt will prove to be a resilient emerging market. I'm not concerned about even a very stiff correction, given the fundamental direction of this market," he added.
